title: North American birds (1969-2024) and British butterflies changed range occupancy more than full thermal tracking needs, but only 4-6% followed temperature; fast life history did not raise it
abstract: Question: earlier campaign work proposed that short generations and high mobility give near-full climate tracking (plankton, moths), so demographic and dispersal limits set the weak tracking of other taxa. We tested this inside surveys with one estimator. Data: North American Breeding Bird Survey 10-stop data (352 species, 1,740 routes; 1969-1988 vs 2005-2024), UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (44 taxa, 289 sites; 1980-1999 vs 2005-2024), Berkeley Earth and E-OBS temperature, AVONET and Amniote traits. Method: per species, a cross-fitted logistic spatial occupancy curve on temperature (plus longitude) predicts the occupancy change from observed warming; transfer theta is the slope of observed on predicted change with species, route and logit-shift terms removed (1 = full transfer). Post hoc: split-half covariance gives the noise-free spatially structured change; its ratio to the full-transfer change is the capacity; a species-swap null tests alignment; cold- and warm-margin slopes are fitted separately. Results: theta was 0.084 (95% CI 0.028-0.153) in birds and 0.087 (0.057-0.119) in butterflies. Bird species changed their spatial occupancy pattern by a median 4.3 times the change that full transfer needs (97% of species above 1); butterflies 0.79. Only 3.8% (birds) and 6.3% (butterflies) of this structured change followed the temperature prediction (null 2.0% and 2.3%, p = 0.005). Transfer did not rise with shorter generation (slope +0.48 per log10 year, -0.16 to 1.11; the cross-survey idea needs about -0.38), larger clutch or higher hand-wing index. Residents carried the bird signal, but about 70% of their cold-margin gain was margin infilling that also occurred at warm margins; long-distance migrants showed none. Butterflies changed at both margins in the thermal direction. Conclusion: the tracking gap is mainly one of direction, not rate: species change a lot, but mostly not along temperature. Limitations: detection change remains in the structured change; theta measures only the differential (margin-contrast) part; curve form changes theta (0.01-0.23); post hoc tests; GB-internal butterfly curves.

citations.reason: We test its proposal that short generations and high mobility explain full transfer; inside birds, transfer did not rise with faster life history or dispersal.
Our species transfer agrees with its small network transfer and its conclusion that the gap is not a long lag.
Membership change carries the gap; we show that membership change is large but mostly not thermal.
Warm-affinity gains without cold-affinity losses; we find bird gains at both margins of species curves.
Bird species-level transfer of 5-14%; we obtain 8% with a different estimator.
British butterfly within-species occupancy transfer of about 10%; we obtain 9%.
Birds follow land-cover gradients weakly too; consistent with direction-limited change.
Distance to a warmer climate did not limit bird tracking; with our capacity result, dispersal distance is not the binding limit.
Winter climate did not close the community gap; our winter variant did not raise resident transfer.
Forest type explained part of the gap on forested routes.
